title: Methods of quantifying mass mortality in freshwater wildlife within river ecosystems
author: Marchowski, Szlauer-Łukaszewska, et al.

steps.title: Prepare mussel decomposition experiment
steps.instruction: Humanely euthanize mussels according to national guidelines, place each in an artificial water basin, adjust water temperature to match the natural habitat, and add a sediment substrate (sandy, muddy, or rocky) that reflects the river environment of the disaster.

steps.title: Collect live mussels and snails
steps.instruction: At designated sampling points, divers equipped with flashlights collect mussels directly from the riverbed while a net with a standardized hydrobiological mesh (consistent inlet width and mesh size) is used simultaneously to capture both mussels and water snails; calculate densities and express them as individuals per 1 m².

steps.title: Observe dead mussels via strip transect
steps.instruction: Along the river mainstream, establish a line perpendicular to the shoreline and use the strip‑transect method to record all dead Unionidae mussels visible on the water surface as they pass the line.

steps.title: Correct counts for detectability
steps.instruction: Apply the detection‑rate correction using the formula x̄ = [(1/n) ∑_{i=1}^{n} x_i / ω] / 5, where x_i is the count in sample i, n is the number of samples, and ω is the average detection rate (assumed arbitrary).

steps.title: Extrapolate to daily mortality estimate
steps.instruction: Multiply the corrected per‑minute count by the number of minutes in a day (1440) to obtain a daily estimate; calculate 95 % confidence intervals for the estimate.

steps.title: Estimate mussel transport distance
steps.instruction: Using measured river current speed, calculate the potential distance a mussel could have traveled from its origin to the survey point.

steps.title: Survey washed‑ashore mussels on banks
steps.instruction: Randomly select ten‑meter transects along the target river section and count dead mussels on the banks; record site (transect location) and river‑kilometer for each transect.

steps.title: Model mussel counts with GAM
steps.instruction: Fit a Generalized Additive Model (GAM) to the transect counts using site and river‑kilometer as predictor variables to explore non‑linear relationships.

steps.title: Model change with GEE
steps.instruction: Apply a Generalized Estimating Equations (GEE) model to the GAM‑predicted values to calculate the average rate of change in mussel numbers across successive river sections and to predict counts for the entire river section.

steps.title: Extrapolate total mussel mortality
steps.instruction: Compute the mean count per transect: x̄ = (1/n) ∑_{i=1}^{n} x_i; then extrapolate to the whole river using x̂ = 2 L x̄, where L is the total river length; assume mussels occupy a 20‑m strip on each side of the riverbed (total width 40 m). Multiply river length by this width to obtain habitat area and then by average mussel density to estimate total population before and after the disaster.

steps.title: Photograph and annotate dead fauna
steps.instruction: Take random photographs of riverbanks that capture representative dead animals (fish, mussels, water snails); annotate the images in a format suitable for neural‑network training.

steps.title: Analyze photos with grid counting
steps.instruction: Superimpose a square grid on each annotated photo, correct for perspective, draw a demarcation line if necessary and exclude objects beyond it; count snails within the grid, compare the average snail count to the mussel count, and calculate dead snail numbers proportionally to the estimated dead mussels.

steps.title: Survey vertebrate mortality along transects
steps.instruction: Select random 10‑m long transects that represent all habitat types (stony, gravel, reed‑covered, sandy) along the river valley; within each transect, search for and count all common vertebrates (lampreys, fish, amphibians, birds, mammals) at species or higher taxonomic level.

steps.title: Convert fish counts to biomass
steps.instruction: For fish, obtain average individual size from sample measurements, apply species‑specific conversion factors, and convert the counted number of individuals into total weight for comparison with other reports.

steps.title: Perform statistical tests on population data
steps.instruction: Assess data normality with histograms, Q‑Q plots, and the Shapiro‑Wilk test; if data are normal, conduct a one‑way ANOVA, otherwise use a Kruskal‑Wallis test to compare population densities, percentages, and frequencies across time points; additionally, use Kruskal‑Wallis and GAM to examine relationships between fish abundance and location.

steps.title: Run R scripts for analysis
steps.instruction: Execute the publicly available R scripts (hosted in the Zenodo repository) on the raw data (available in the Mendeley repository) to reproduce all statistical analyses, model fittings, and visualizations described above.
